cards.headline: Officers unfamiliar with skimmers check all pumps at Fort Pierce 7-Eleven
cards.teaser: After a cybersecurity professional discovered a card skimmer at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, responding officers checked every pump at the station. Neither the manager nor the officers had seen a skimmer in person before.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional discovered a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation in which officers checked every pump at the station. Arlo Bess, who has 25 years of cybersecurity experience, found the device after routinely pulling on the card reader before pumping gas. Neither the store manager nor the responding officers had ever seen a skimmer in person before.

 Bess stopped at the station on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 while heading back to Palm Bay. He said he has tugged on card readers at gas stations for years as a precaution, and this was the first time one came loose. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the manager, who called police. Officers arrived within minutes, took a report, and worked with Bess to check all the other pumps.

 Bess explained that skimmers take only two to three seconds to install or remove and are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads data from a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. Thieves typically leave devices in place for about a week to collect card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes, then sell the information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards for use at self-checkout kiosks or online purchases.

 Bess said consumers cannot reliably spot a skimmer just by looking and that the best check is a firm pull on the card reader without using tools. He recommends tapping cards or paying inside instead, and avoiding debit cards at the pump because fraud protections differ from credit cards and it can take weeks to recover stolen money from a checking account. For debit or ATM cards, he suggests using machines inside bank lobbies because outdoor machines are easier targets. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA gives Cadence at Tradition homeowners Sept. 30 deadline to replace dead trees
cards.teaser: Residents in the Cadence at Tradition community received letters from their homeowners association demanding they replace dead trees by Sept. 30 or face escalation. Homeowners say the trees are on easements and should be the HOA's responsibility.
cards.body:
Residents in Cadence at Tradition in Port St. Lucie received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding they replace dead trees on their property by Sept. 30 or face escalation. The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not comply.

 The letter states that assistance and cooperation are requested regarding landscaping and dead trees. Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners.

 Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

 The letter states that the deceased tree or trees on their property are in need of attention and kindly requests residents address the matter by Sept. 30 to avoid escalation.

cards.headline: Officers unfamiliar with skimmers check all pumps at Fort Pierce 7-Eleven
cards.teaser: After a cybersecurity professional discovered a card skimmer at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, responding officers checked every pump at the station. Neither the manager nor the officers had seen a skimmer in person before.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional discovered a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation in which officers checked every pump at the station. Arlo Bess, who has 25 years of cybersecurity experience, found the device after routinely pulling on the card reader before pumping gas. Neither the store manager nor the responding officers had ever seen a skimmer in person before.

 Bess stopped at the station on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 while heading back to Palm Bay. He said he has tugged on card readers at gas stations for years as a precaution, and this was the first time one came loose. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the manager, who called police. Officers arrived within minutes, took a report, and worked with Bess to check all the other pumps.

 Bess explained that skimmers take only two to three seconds to install or remove and are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads data from a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. Thieves typically leave devices in place for about a week to collect card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes, then sell the information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards for use at self-checkout kiosks or online purchases.

 Bess said consumers cannot reliably spot a skimmer just by looking and that the best check is a firm pull on the card reader without using tools. He recommends tapping cards or paying inside instead, and avoiding debit cards at the pump because fraud protections differ from credit cards and it can take weeks to recover stolen money from a checking account. For debit or ATM cards, he suggests using machines inside bank lobbies because outdoor machines are easier targets. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA gives Cadence at Tradition homeowners Sept. 30 deadline to replace dead trees
cards.teaser: Residents in the Cadence at Tradition community received letters from their homeowners association demanding they replace dead trees by Sept. 30 or face escalation. Homeowners say the trees are on easements and should be the HOA's responsibility.
cards.body:
Residents in Cadence at Tradition in Port St. Lucie received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding they replace dead trees on their property by Sept. 30 or face escalation. The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not comply.

 The letter states that assistance and cooperation are requested regarding landscaping and dead trees. Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners.

 Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

 The letter states that the deceased tree or trees on their property are in need of attention and kindly requests residents address the matter by Sept. 30 to avoid escalation.
